title: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), Policy Gradient / PPO, Action Chunking & Sim-to-Real Safety Wrappers

blocks.x: 1. Why it matters

This is the final bridge module in the Track 06 Tier 3 Embodied AI ladder before Step 3.7 (`06-robotics.T3.07`). While Behavior Cloning (`06-robotics.T3.06a`) imitates human demonstrations, **Reinforcement Learning (RL / PPO)** discovers agile locomotion and contact behaviors in GPU simulators (`Newton`, `Isaac Lab`, `MuJoCo Playground`) by maximizing discounted cumulative reward $G_t = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma^k r_{t+k}$. And to deploy *either* an RL policy or a Vision-Language-Action (`VLA` / `ACT` / `Diffusion` / `π₀`) policy onto real $48\text{ V}$ hardware without violent jitter or collisions, you must master **Action Chunking with Temporal Ensembling / Real-Time Chunking (`RTC`)**, **Domain Randomization**, and a hard $1\text{ kHz}$ **Sim-to-Real CBF/Impedance Safety Shield**. Already know this? Read `### Safety notes` first, then take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7.
2. Intuition first

blocks.caption: State, action, reward: the reward is the only teacher.

blocks.x: In supervised learning (`06-robotics.T3.06a`), a teacher tells the network the exact right action $a_t^*$ on every step. In **Reinforcement Learning (MDP)**, there is no teacher—only a scoreboard (the **reward function** $r_t$, which awards points for reaching the goal and deducts points for excessive torque or falling over). The policy tries actions, sees which rollouts scored higher than expected (positive **Advantage** $\hat{A}_t > 0$), and increases the log-probability of those winning actions while **PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)** clips the update ratio $r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}}$ to $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$ so one lucky rollout doesn't wreck the policy! Second, why do modern manipulation policies (`ACT`, `Diffusion Policy`, `π₀`) predict a whole **chunk of $K=16$ future waypoints** instead of a single step, and blend overlapping chunks with exponential weights $w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$ (**Temporal Ensembling / Real-Time Chunking**)? Because blending overlapping predictions smooths out frame-to-frame camera noise and bridges the $30\text{–}100\text{ ms}$ vision inference delay! Finally, because a neural network can output an arbitrary wild number if given an out-of-distribution camera image, **never** wire a neural network directly to raw motor voltage—always wrap it inside a $1\text{ kHz}$ **Safety Shield** that clamps joint step size $|\Delta q_{\text{cmd}}| \le \Delta q_{\max}$, joint limits, and Control Barrier Function (`CBF-QP`) workspace walls!

items.x: **Action Chunking & Temporal Ensembling (`ACT` / `RTC`):** At inference step $t$, the policy outputs a chunk of $K$ future target positions $\hat{A}_t = [\hat{a}_{t\mid t},\ \hat{a}_{t+1\mid t},\ \dots,\ \hat{a}_{t+K-1\mid t}]$. Thus for current time $t$, we have $M \le K$ overlapping predictions $\hat{a}_{t\mid t-i}$ made $i \in \{0, \dots, M-1\}$ steps ago. **Sim-to-Real Domain Randomization & $1\text{ kHz}$ Safety Wrapper:**
**Domain Randomization:** Randomizing link mass $m \sim \mathcal{U}[0.8m_0, 1.2m_0]$, friction, and latency $\tau_d$ during GPU training forces $\pi_\theta$ to learn robust feedback strategies.
**Deterministic Safety Shield:** Before any policy action $a_t^{\text{ens}}$ reaches the $1\text{ kHz}$ PD/impedance controller, hardware-enforced safety wrapper projects it into safe bounds:

Use & Understand

This level is for the learner deploying a policy, not deriving PPO. Four tools, each with a clear moment: the **discounted return** turns a reward sequence into one score per step; **PPO's clipped surrogate** raises the probability of actions whose advantage $\hat{A}_t = G_t - V(s_t)$ beat the value estimate, but never by more than the trust region allows; **action chunking with temporal ensembling** keeps the $1\,\text{kHz}$ controller fed while a $30$–$50\,\text{Hz}$ vision model thinks; and the **safety shield** is the deterministic wrapper that runs whether or not the policy is sane. Reach for RL when no demonstration shows the behaviour but a reward can score it; reach for chunking whenever inference latency exceeds one control tick; never deploy without the shield.

Derive & Extend
Level B earns the three formulas section 3 states.

items.x: **The return recursion is the geometric series, factored.** By definition, and then by re-indexing the tail:

blocks.tex: G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1} \gamma^k r_{t+k} = r_t + \gamma \sum_{k=1}^{T-t-1} \gamma^{k-1} r_{t+k} = r_t + \gamma G_{t+1}

blocks.x: With $G_T = 0$, evaluating from the last reward backwards is exact and costs one multiply-add per step, which is why no rollout sum is ever computed forwards.

items.x: **Generalised advantage estimation is that recursion with a bootstrapped tail.** With the temporal-difference error $\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$ and trace parameter $\lambda \in [0, 1]$, define $\hat{A}_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda \hat{A}_{t+1}$. Unrolling $L$ steps gives $\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{L-1} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}$, so at $\lambda = 0$ only the first term survives and $\hat{A}_t = \delta_t$ - the one-step TD error - while at $\lambda = 1$ the telescoping sum collapses to $\sum_l \gamma^l r_{t+l} - V(s_t) = G_t - V(s_t)$, the Monte-Carlo advantage of section 3 item 1. Every intermediate $\lambda$ is a variance-bias dial between the two.

**The clipped objective's gradient vanishes where the clip binds.** Write $\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)$ and hold $\hat{A}_t$ fixed. Since $\operatorname{clip}(\rho, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)$ is constant outside its band, its derivative is zero there, and for $\hat{A}_t > 0$ the pessimistic $\min$ selects the clipped branch once $\rho > 1+\epsilon$; for $\hat{A}_t < 0$ it selects it once $\rho < 1-\epsilon$. Hence

blocks.x: so a step that would leave the trust region contributes no gradient at all, and the update is driven only by in-band ratios times $\partial \log \pi_\theta / \partial \theta$.

items.x: **Temporal ensembling is a convex combination.** The weights $w_i = \exp(-m i)$ are positive for every $m \ge 0$, so the coefficients $w_i / \sum_j w_j$ are non-negative and sum to $1$, and $a_t^{\text{ens}} = \sum_i w_i \hat{a}_{t \mid t-i} / \sum_i w_i$ is a convex combination; therefore $\min_i \hat{a}_{t \mid t-i} \le a_t^{\text{ens}} \le \max_i \hat{a}_{t \mid t-i}$, and at $m = 0$ every weight is $1$ and the formula reduces to the arithmetic mean. This is why the ensemble cannot invent an action no chunk predicted - a property the safety shield still has to enforce on the joint.

blocks.x: **Extend.** Real-time chunking re-plans while the previous chunk is still executing. Write the ensemble with the window cut at $K - d$ for a delay of $d$ ticks, and show how the weights shift when a fresh age-zero prediction replaces the oldest weight $\exp(-m(M-1))$; then state the condition on $m$ under which the newest chunk still dominates.
4. Worked example

**Predict first (before you run it):** Commit to four numbers before the code runs. (1) With rewards $[1.0, 2.0, 4.0]$ and $\gamma = 0.90$, is $G_0$ closer to $7.0$ or to $4.0$ - and what is $G_1$? (2) For $\rho = 1.50$, $\hat{A} = +2.0$ and $\epsilon = 0.20$, does the pessimistic $\min$ return $3.00$ or $2.40$? (3) Blending $[0.52, 0.50, 0.46]$ with $m = 0.5$: does the result land closer to the newest or to the oldest prediction? (4) With $q = 0.50\text{ rad}$, $\Delta q_{\max} = 0.08\text{ rad}$ and $q_{\max} = 1.5\text{ rad}$, what does the shield output for a policy asking $+2.80\text{ rad}$? Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a different convention: a ratio of $1.50$ may not survive as a multiplier once it is outside $[0.80, 1.20]$, so an unclipped $3.00$ means the clip was skipped; and the shield output must be exactly $\Delta q_{\max}$ from the measured $q$, so an answer that jumps to $2.80$ or slides to $1.50$ applied the rate limit on the wrong side or skipped the joint-limit clamp.

Compute the discounted return $G_0$, evaluate the PPO clipped objective for an overly large probability ratio $\rho = 1.50$ ($\epsilon = 0.20$), blend 3 overlapping action chunks via Temporal Ensembling ($m = 0.5$), and verify that the Sim-to-Real Safety Wrapper clamps an out-of-distribution policy spike before it can jerk the joint.

blocks.text:
import math

def discounted_return(rewards: list[float], gamma: float = 0.90) -> list[float]:
    G = [0.0] * len(rewards)
    running = 0.0
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):
        running = rewards[t] + gamma * running
        G[t] = running
    return G

G = discounted_return([1.0, 2.0, 4.0], gamma=0.90)
assert math.isclose(G[0], 1.0 + 0.9 * 2.0 + 0.81 * 4.0, rel_tol=1e-9)  # 6.04

def ppo_clip_term(rho: float, adv: float, eps: float = 0.20) -> float:
    rho_clipped = max(1.0 - eps, min(1.0 + eps, rho))
    return min(rho * adv, rho_clipped * adv)

assert math.isclose(ppo_clip_term(rho=1.50, adv=2.0, eps=0.20), 1.20 * 2.0, rel_tol=1e-9)

# Temporal ensembling of 3 overlapping predictions for step t (i=0 newest, i=1, i=2 oldest):
preds_for_t = [0.52, 0.50, 0.46]
weights = [math.exp(-0.5 * i) for i in range(len(preds_for_t))]
a_ens = sum(w * p for w, p in zip(weights, preds_for_t)) / sum(weights)
assert 0.46 < a_ens < 0.52

# Sim-to-Real Safety Shield: current q = 0.50 rad, wild policy output = +2.80 rad!
def safety_shield(a_policy: float, q_curr: float, dq_max: float = 0.08,
                  q_min: float = -1.5, q_max: float = 1.5) -> float:
    q_rate_limited = max(q_curr - dq_max, min(q_curr + dq_max, a_policy))
    return max(q_min, min(q_max, q_rate_limited))

q_safe = safety_shield(a_policy=2.80, q_curr=0.50, dq_max=0.08)
assert math.isclose(q_safe, 0.58, rel_tol=1e-9)
print(f"G_0={G[0]:.2f}, PPO_clip={ppo_clip_term(1.5, 2.0):.2f}, a_ens={a_ens:.4f} rad, q_safe={q_safe:.2f} rad")

blocks.x: 5. Exercise

Suppose a reward sequence is $r = [0.0, 0.0, 10.0]$ over 3 steps with discount factor $\gamma = 0.95$, and at step $t=0$ the PPO probability ratio is $\rho_0 = 0.60$ with negative advantage $\hat{A}_0 = -3.0$ and clip range $\epsilon = 0.20$. Compute $G_0 = \gamma^2 (10.0)$ and the clipped PPO objective $\min(\rho_0 \hat{A}_0,\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_0, 0.8, 1.2)\hat{A}_0)$. Verify $G_0 = 9.025$ and $L^{\text{CLIP}}_0 = \min(-1.80, -2.40) = -2.40$ ($\pm 10^{-9}$).

items.x: **If your result differs:** When $\hat{A}_0 < 0$ and $\rho_0 = 0.60 < 0.80$, $\rho_0 \hat{A}_0 = -1.80$ while the clipped term is $0.80 \times (-3.0) = -2.40$; taking the pessimistic $\min(-1.80, -2.40)$ gives $-2.40$.

[`exercises/06-robotics.T3.06b/`](../exercises/06-robotics.T3.06b/) turns this section into a test. `starter.py` holds seven holes: `discounted_returns` (the backward recursion), `advantages`, `ppo_clip_term` (the pessimistic minimum), `ppo_loss` (its batch mean), `temporal_ensemble` (exponential weights, newest first), `safety_shield` (step clamp then joint limit) and `watchdog_trip` (strictly past the timeout). Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

**28 tests.** The returns are checked at more than $G_0$ - $G_1$ and $G_2$ catch a discount taken from the start of the rollout; the PPO term is checked on a **negative** advantage, where the correct $\min$ is the more pessimistic number and a `max` silently doubles the step; the ensemble is checked at zero decay (the plain mean) and at large decay (the newest prediction dominates); the shield is checked where the step clamp would walk past a joint limit; and the watchdog is checked at exactly the timeout and after a long run that keeps sending chunks. The transfer suite scores **the plant's own run**: the discounted return of its tracking errors must equal a brute-force sum at $t = 0, 1, 7$ and halfway; the plant's own targets pass through the shield with $<2\%$ RMS change; and a hostile policy commanding $+3\text{ rad}$ through the shield leaves the arm inside its joint range, slow, and never more than $\Delta q_{\max}$ from where it is. Five planted faults - `gamma_from_zero`, `ppo_max_not_min`, `ensemble_uniform`, `shield_no_joint_limit`, `watchdog_compares_absolute_time` - each fail the test named for them.

Hint ladder

items.x: **Discount from the step, not the start.** $G_t = r_t + \gamma G_{t+1}$ run from $t = 2$ backwards gives $G_2 = 10.0$, $G_1 = 9.5$, $G_0 = 0.95 \times 9.5 = 9.025$ - discounting $[0, 0, 10]$ from $t = 0$ instead gives $10 \times 0.95^2$ for every entry and hides the bug.

**Why the pessimistic `min` binds only outside the trust region.** With $\rho = 0.60$ and $\hat{A} = -3.0$: the raw product is $-1.80$, the clipped ratio $0.80$ gives $-2.40$, and `min` keeps $-2.40$. For a *negative* advantage the pessimistic choice is the more negative number, which is why `max` looks harmless on the worked positive case.

**Weights are newest-first and normalised.** $w_i = e^{-m i}$ starts at $1$ for `predictions[0]`; dividing by $\sum w_i$ is what makes a zero decay reduce to the plain mean, and a large decay let the newest prediction dominate.

**Order matters in the shield.** Step-clamp around the *measured* $q$ first, then apply the joint limits: at $q = -1.45$, $\Delta q_{\max} = 0.10$ and a $-2.00$ command the rate limit already reaches $-1.55$, so only the second clamp keeps you inside $[-1.50, +1.50]$.

**What the suite refuses.** `discounted_returns` refuses a discount of one and an empty rollout; `advantages` refuses a reward/advantage length mismatch; `ppo_clip_term` refuses a clip range without `low < high` (a non-positive `eps` included) and a non-positive ratio; `ppo_loss` refuses ratio and advantage lists of different lengths; `temporal_ensemble` refuses an empty chunk and a negative decay; `safety_shield` refuses a zero step clamp and inverted position limits; and `watchdog_trip` refuses a non-positive timeout. All raise `ValueError`.

blocks.x: Break it on purpose

blocks.caption: A fault caught on the bench costs minutes; the same fault in the demo costs the demo.

blocks.x: Inject the `ppo_max_not_min` fault and diagnose it from the loss alone, keeping $\epsilon = 0.20$ and $\hat{A} = +2.0$ for the positive case:

items.x: **Inject:** replace the pessimistic `min` in the clipped surrogate with `max`, i.e. `max(rho * adv, rho_clipped * adv)`, which is the single most common transcription slip in PPO code.

**Symptom:** the positive-advantage case silently grows from $2.40$ to $3.00$ - a $25\%$ larger step for a ratio the clip was meant to reject - and the negative-advantage exercise case with $\rho_0 = 0.60$ and $\hat{A}_0 = -3.0$ returns $-1.80$ instead of $-2.40$, so the policy is punished $0.60$ less for a ratio outside the trust region. Training still runs and the loss still falls, which is why the fault survives a smoke test.

**Diagnose:** the sign of the advantage separates it from a discount or ensemble bug. With $\hat{A} > 0$ the `max` equals the raw product whenever $\rho > 1.20$, and with $\hat{A} < 0$ it equals the raw product whenever $\rho < 0.80$ - in both cases the term stops tracking the clipped product exactly where the clip should bind, while the returns $G_0$ and $G_1$ remain correct.

**Fix:** restore `min(rho * adv, rho_clipped * adv)` and prove it on the two cases that disagree: $(1.50, +2.0)$ must give $2.40$, and $(0.60, -3.0)$ must give $-2.40$ rather than $-1.80$. `test_behavior`'s negative-advantage case and `test_transfer`'s return check must both pass, and the planted fault must fail the test named for it.

Safety notes

**⚠️ Mandatory Safety Briefing (`safety_level: high` — read before deploying any learned policy on hardware or taking the Skip/Gate test):**
1. **Never Wire a Neural Policy Directly to Raw Motor Voltage/Current:** A neural network (`BC`, `PPO`, `Diffusion`, `VLA`) has no mathematical guarantee against outputting extreme actions when encountering a camera glare, occlusion, or out-of-distribution state. Every learned policy output **must** pass through a deterministic $1\text{ kHz}$ low-level **Safety Shield** (`safety_shield` + CBF-QP + joint PD torque clamp) running on the real-time controller.
2. **Per-Tick Slew-Rate / Step Clamping (`dq_max`):** Clamp the maximum position deviation $|q_d - q_{\text{meas}}| \le \Delta q_{\max}$ (e.g., $\le 0.05\text{–}0.10\text{ rad}$), velocity $|\dot{q}_d| \le \dot{q}_{\max}$, and torque $|\tau| \le \tau_{\max}$ on every tick, and trip into hardware Safe Torque Off (`STO` / `FAULT`) if the policy heartbeat times out ($> 100\text{ ms}$).
3. **Physical E-Stop in Hand During First Policy Rollout:** Always keep a physical hardware E-stop button in hand and test new checkpoints at $25\%$ torque ceiling in a clear workspace before full-speed evaluation.

`[Transfer] [Concept: action_chunking_temporal_ensembling_rtc]` Why do modern visuomotor policies (`ACT`, `Diffusion Policy`, `π₀` with Real-Time Chunking `RTC`) predict a chunk of $K = 16\text{–}50$ future actions at once and blend overlapping chunks rather than predicting a single action $a_t$ independently at each frame?
**A.** To use more GPU memory.

**B.** To eliminate non-Markovian human pauses, smooth out high-frequency action jitter across frames, and maintain continuous $1\text{ kHz}$ execution even while the next vision inference takes $30\text{–}80\text{ ms}$.
**C.** Because cameras only capture 1 image per minute.
**D.** To disable the joint encoders.

`[SAFETY] [Concept: sim_to_real_domain_randomization_and_safety_shield]` A vision-language-action (`VLA`) policy running at $30\text{ Hz}$ suffers a camera glare and suddenly outputs a joint target of $q_{\text{policy}} = +3.14\text{ rad}$ while the robot arm is at $q = 0.20\text{ rad}$. If the $1\text{ kHz}$ safety shield enforces a maximum step clamp $\Delta q_{\max} = 0.06\text{ rad}$ around $q$, what safe target $q_d$ in radians (tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}$) is passed to the PD controller?

`[SAFETY] [Concept: sim_to_real_domain_randomization_and_safety_shield]` What must the $1\text{ kHz}$ real-time motor controller do if the $30\text{ Hz}$ GPU policy process crashes or stops sending action chunks for more than the watchdog timeout ($100\text{ ms}$)?
**A.** Continue extrapolating the last velocity forever until the arm hits the table.
**B.** Immediately transition to a safe hold/damped-stop trajectory (`qd_des = 0`, hold current $q$ or engage STO) and raise a communication timeout fault.

head: Symptom
Root cause
2-minute fix
rows: RL policy achieves huge reward in simulation by vibrating joints at $500text{ Hz}$, then shakes real hardware to pieces
Reward function omitted action-rate penalty $-alpha |a_t - a_{t-1}|^2$ and torque penalty $-beta |tau_t|^2$.
Always penalize action smoothness $|a_t - a_{t-1}|^2$, joint velocity, and torque in the training reward, and randomize actuator delay in sim.
Arm pauses for $50text{ ms}$ every $K=16$ steps at the boundary between action chunks
Executed an entire chunk open-loop to completion before starting the next camera inference.
Run inference every $d < K$ steps asynchronously and blend overlapping chunks with Temporal Ensembling / Real-Time Chunking (`RTC`, `arXiv:2506.07339`).
Joint sign or gear offset in real robot differs from `MuJoCo`/`Isaac` model, causing instant runaway on policy start
Mismatched joint zero offset or axis sign between sim URDF and `ros2_control` hardware interface.
Verify in a passive gravity-comp mode that moving each real joint $+0.2text{ rad}$ moves the simulated twin's joint in the exact same direction before enabling policy output.
